elements.text: Ticker: EVO SS
Share price: SEK726
Target price: SEK610
Mkt cap: SEK146bn
20 October 2025
Evolution AB
Winter of Discontent

Thesis: A year ago, investors were expecting a 2H25-weighted inflection in growth as Evolution digested the twin growth headwinds of Asian cyberattacks and European ‘ringfencing’. But in our view, cyberattacks have now become a ‘forever war’, while our work suggests that further ringfencing headwinds are to come. We see downside risks to 2026E consensus expectations of a return to double-digit revenue growth.

No ‘Sommar’ at all – ‘Winter of Discontent’ instead. Our recent catch-up with Evolution suggested mixed trends (at best) during 3Q25. Early signs of stabilisation in Europe are potentially encouraging, but a recovery in Asian revenue growth remains distant. North American market growth remains tilted towards Evolution’s weak spot (random number generator (RNG) slots), while Latin America has promise, despite signs of near-term softness in Brazil.

‘Tom & Jerry’ in Asia: Evolution’s own ‘forever war’. Evolution characterised the impact of its cyberattack countermeasures as a bit of a ‘cat and mouse’ game – the bad actors hijacking the Evolution feed simply find ways to circumvent the new countermeasures implemented by the company. To us, the much hoped for revenue growth recovery in Asia remains as distant as ever. Meanwhile, gambling crackdowns in Asia continue at pace and add structural headwinds.

European ringfencing checks indicate Evolution has fallen behind peers. Our latest ringfencing checks in Europe have been expanded to examine the extent of Evolution’s ringfencing compared to other large industry peers such as Hacksaw Gaming (Not Rated) and Pragmatic Play (Not Listed). We see risks of Evolution ringfencing doubling from just seven countries to 14 in Europe – we do not believe this has been factored into consensus estimates.

Reiterate Sell (price target: SEK610) – recent consensus cuts are not enough. We argue that rebased consensus growth expectations still imply rebounds in group revenue growth to 9% and 10% in 2026E and 2027E respectively. But, for the reasons outlined above, we continue to see risks to consensus estimates. We trim our EBITDA estimates by 1%/3%/3% in 2025E/2026E/2027E, reflecting the more modest top-line trends. We reiterate our Sell rating and lower our price target to SEK610 (from SEK650).

elements.text: Winter of our discontent
Earlier this month, we had a catch-up with the company discussing recent developments within the Evolution business. It is fair to say that trends remain mixed:

Asia continues to be impacted by the cyberattacks/hijacking, where Evolution’s countermeasures are gradually circumvented. The company described its efforts here as a bit of a game of ‘cat and mouse’. To us, it appears that a reacceleration of revenue growth in Asia remains a far-off prospect.

In Europe, the company expects some sequential improvement into 2H25 as the ringfencing takes hold. However, our ringfencing work in this report suggests that incremental headwinds continue to loom, with at least a further seven EU countries potentially subject to incremental ringfencing.

In Latin America, Evolution remains at the mercy of the softer than expected market start in Brazil despite its longer-term promise. The company characterised the market as positive, despite being slow growing. This corresponds with recent commentary from Entain (Buy) management, which suggested that iGaming remains soft in Brazil, with recent growth being led largely by sports betting.
In North America, the company has conceded that it remains a slots-driven market, and that the focus has turned to improving the RNG product in order to drive growth in the region.
Asia headwinds: no end in sight
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: To us, it appears that the revenue growth inflection in Asia is further away than ever – cyberattacks and gambling crackdowns are continuing to impact the business.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: As a reminder, we remain sceptical about the impact that cyberattacks and hijacking are having on Evolution’s Asian business. In ‘Regulatory Revolution’ (17 January 2025), we argued that there was likely a confluence of both cyclical (cyberattacks) and structural (gambling crackdown) elements at play.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Nonetheless, the cyberattack narrative has now morphed from a cyclical/transitory one to a ‘forever war’, where revenue headwinds continue to impact the business as Evolution’s countermeasures are eventually circumvented by the content hijackers.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: On the structural elements, as we discussed in ‘Not Yet Sommar’ (24 July 2025), the regulatory crackdowns on online gambling continue across numerous jurisdictions, with the following developments over recent weeks:
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: In Japan, on top of the previously reported arrests of end players, authorities have reportedly taken action against online casino advertising. There have been a number of developments:
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Two individuals were arrested for promoting offshore gambling and receiving commissions from gambling sites, as authorities begin to target online affiliates in the country. This follows new laws that came into effect on 25 September 2025 that ban online casinos and prohibit social media platforms and websites from displaying gambling ads.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Moreover, authorities have even gone as far as appealing to regulators in Malta, Costa Rica, Georgia, Anjouan and Curaçao, among others, to seek assistance in curbing illegal online gambling offered by overseas operators in Japan. This mirrors efforts from regulators in Australia, which has sought similar assistance from overseas jurisdictions.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: South Korea has shut down an illegal online gambling operation that was based in Cambodia, which reportedly handled as much as KRW44bn in gambling flows. Ten individuals were arrested and a further 174 who played the games were charged. Games allegedly played included Baccarat.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: In India, which recently passed a new law banning all forms of real money gaming, the Enforcement Directorate of India has taken steps to seize funds linked to illegal online gambling in the country – targeting various sports stars and well-known actors who were reportedly gambling on 1xBet. Evolution content is indeed available on 1xBet, while our industry contacts noted that the content was being distributed into the country via aggregators such as Diamond Exchange and BollyTech.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Vietnamese authorities have reportedly jailed as many as 43 people in a $3.8bn illegal gambling case linked to crypto and money laundering, with offences dating back as far as 2020-21.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: In Malaysia, the gambling crackdowns continue, with 328 arrested in a large-scale operation as recently as August 2025.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Philippines banned the Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGOs) more than a year ago and continues its crackdown on operators that have failed to heed the new laws. 91 illegal Chinese workers were deported with China’s cooperation.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Indonesia has reportedly taken down up to 2.8 million posts on social media and online forums linked to illegal online gambling in the country since October 2024.
section_path: Asia headwinds: no end in sight

elements.text: Regulatory ringfencing update

Our ringfencing updates show no material changes on the surface. The seven EU countries where Evolution appears to ringfence its products are: Czech Republic, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Netherlands, Romania and Sweden. The well-documented UK Gambling Commission (UKGC) licence review also sees the UK as an eighth European market where Evolution ringfences.

However, we have expanded upon our checks to include peer B2B suppliers Hacksaw Gaming (Not Rated) and Pragmatic Play (Not Listed) in a comparison versus Evolution. This draws out some interesting observations with respect to potential incremental ringfencing risks for Evolution (Fig 3).

elements.caption: Evolution ringfencing checks – availability of Evolution content by EU country
elements.note: Note: ringfencing checks are conducted via a broad selection of offshore cryptocasino operators including Snatch Casino, BC Game, stake.com, 7Bit casino, shuffle.com, freshbet, boomerang casino, wazamba, sportsbet.io, bitcasino.io and toshi.bet

elements.text: While there are some cases like Denmark where availability is consistently restricted across all three suppliers, we note several examples of EU countries where Hacksaw and/or Pragmatic Play have chosen to ringfence their content and limit supply to the unregulated crypto casino channel, but where Evolution content remains available. We regard these jurisdictions as potentially at risk of incremental ringfencing at Evolution, driven by more onerous regulatory enforcement.

There are a further seven EU markets where either Hacksaw or Pragmatic Play has decided to restrict its content, yet where Evolution’s content is freely available. These markets are Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Italy, Lithuania, Malta and Spain.
Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: In Italy, we were able to access Evolution content on six out of 12 unregulated sites checked (Fig 4). However, our extended ringfencing checks observed that other competitor B2B suppliers are beginning to ringfence and restrict supply.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Notably, for reasons that remain unclear, our checks suggest that Pragmatic Play has begun to restrict supply from most unregulated sites in Italy (with the sole exception of the Soft2bet-linked Boomerang casino).
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: Italy supplier/operator ringfencing matrix
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Consistent with several other sites, Pragmatic Play’s live dealer content appears to have been subject to supplier-side ringfencing – shuffle.com displays the below message following attempts to launch a Pragmatic Play live dealer game on its platform (Fig 5).
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: Pragmatic Play content ringfenced supply in Italy
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Indeed, Rainbet has already proactively ‘greyed out’ Pragmatic Play live dealer content from its casino lobby (Fig 6), suggesting that this ringfencing has been coordinated with operators. This stands in stark contrast to the broader availability of Evolution games on unregulated sites in Italy.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: In our view, Italy is a good candidate for incremental ringfencing of B2B suppliers driven by regulators. Legitimate operators in the regulated Italian market have just paid €7m for an upfront concession to operate. We suspect that these operators would not have invested an upfront fee 35x higher than the prior concession tender (along with a higher gaming tax rate) without requesting that the regulator crack down on the black market in return.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Ironically, crypto casino stake.com is one operator that has applied for a new concession and operates within the regulated Italian market. Its unregulated ‘.com’ site redirects users to its ‘legitimate’ alternative stake.it site.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: Rainbet’s live dealer casino lobby (October 2025)
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Elsewhere, it appears that other operators have been more proactive than Evolution when it comes to restricting content in other explicitly illegal markets such as France (Fig 7).
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: France supplier/operator ringfencing matrix
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Our ringfencing checks found that Evolution continues to perform no explicit ringfencing for the French market, despite iGaming being illegal in the country. We were able to stream and play Crazy Time via a French IP address as recently as October 2025 using a VPN (Fig 8). Evolution seemingly relies on operators to not serve its content into the French market but does no checks of its own to ensure that it is not supplying its games into the French market.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: In contrast, Pragmatic’s content is not even clickable on stake.com (Fig 9), while the supplier actively blocks its content on other unregulated sites. We found a similar experience with Hacksaw games when using a French IP address via VPN.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: stake.com – Evolution’s Crazy Time continues to be accessible via French IP addresses
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.caption: stake.com – Pragmatic Play content geoblocked on French IP addresses
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Meanwhile in Spain, we found Evolution content available on just one site – Freshbet – indicating that Evolution’s existing ringfencing could be more robust when compared to other suppliers.
section_path: Italy: suppliers are beginning to restrict access

elements.text: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: Consensus revenue expectations have been cut since our 24 July 2025 report, with the downgrades largely coming from Asia (Fig 10). This has correspondingly driven cuts of 4-7% at the EBITDA line between 2026E and 2028E (Fig 11).
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.caption: Evolution consensus revenue estimate changes since 24 July 2025, by geography
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.caption: Evolution consensus EBITDA estimate changes since 24 July 2025
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: However, despite the recent downgrades, consensus continues to expect a revenue reacceleration to 9-10% in 2026E and 2027E, driven by a recovery in both Asia and Europe (Fig 12). Our work in this report suggests that this may be too optimistic:
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: Asia is likely to remain soft in our view, as the ‘forever war’ of cyberattacks and hijacking acts as an ongoing handbrake to Asian growth.
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: Incremental European ringfencing looks increasingly likely, with Evolution ultimately being forced to double the number of countries ringfenced from seven to 14. In our view, consensus has yet to factor this in.
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.caption: Evolution consensus revenue growth (YoY) expectations, 2025E-28E
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: Consequently, we trim our 2025E/2026E/2027E revenue estimates by 1%/2%/2% respectively, reflecting a more modest growth trajectory from 2026E onwards as further incremental ringfencing takes hold in Europe and subdued growth in Asia remains as Evolution’s countermeasures prove ineffective. This leaves us 4% and 5% below consensus revenues in 2026E and 2027E respectively, leading to our estimates being 7% and 10% below consensus at the EBITDA line (Fig 13).
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.caption: Evolution estimate revisions and vs consensus
section_path: Consensus expectations have moderated… but not enough

elements.text: Can Evolution placate shareholders?

We believe Evolution will seek to placate shareholders at 3Q25 results via the announcement of a new c€500m share buyback over and above the existing programme. The existing buyback programme is on track for completion by November 2025 (Fig 14). However, we have not included this in our refreshed estimates.

Furthermore, with the existing Galaxy Gaming (GLXZ) acquisition still subject to a multitude of regulatory approvals (including Nevada), we suspect that Evolution may seek to withdraw from the deal and pivot towards returning the capital to shareholders instead. Galaxy’s share price continues to trade at a material discount to the $3.20/share bid price, implying significant market scepticism that the deal will indeed close during 2H25 (Fig 15).

elements.caption: Cumulative Evolution share buybacks vs announced programme (SEKm)
elements.note: Note: €500m announced buyback programme at spot EUR/SEK rates

elements.caption: Galaxy Gaming share price discount to bid

elements.text: Withdrawing from the GLXZ deal would unlock a further c€100m (c$120m enterprise value) of capital that could be put towards a new share buyback programme in 2026.

However, this would raise a question around the regulatory issues Evolution faced that stalled the deal completion in the first place. If state regulators found reason to stall or delay regulatory approvals for GLXZ, what could this mean for Evolution’s prospects of securing incremental iGaming supplier licences should these same states eventually elect to legalise iGaming?
Consequently, we would regard Evolution’s failure to complete the GLXZ acquisition negatively given the longer-term implications for Evolution’s North American growth prospects.
Reiterate Sell rating
Given our below-consensus earnings estimates, we continue to see downside risk to Evolution’s share price. We cut our target price to SEK610 (from SEK650) and reiterate our Sell rating.

Upside risks to our valuation include a faster than anticipated recovery in growth, led by Asia and Europe. However, our ringfencing checks suggest that this much hoped for growth inflection appears ever distant, and we believe it will begin to test investor patience. We do not believe that a renewed share buyback will be enough to placate shareholders with respect to the possible negative implications for Evolution’s North American growth prospects.
